prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping opened measurement of time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean case of a new regime of measurement physics that has proven robust. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors at once, and Ye's group pushed it to roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty with many-body clock physics and cavity-stabilised lasers. Independent laboratories in Japan, the US, Europe and China now agree at that level and compare their clocks over optical fibre. The result is already used for tests of fundamental constants, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and relativistic geodesy, and it underlies the discussion of redefining the second. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with a two-person prize of a proposer-and-first-demonstrator and the leading realiser. Six of eight members ranked it and five placed it in their top three, which reflects breadth of support, though I weigh the physics and not the count.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier precision-measurement prizes: the 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb and the 2012 prize rewarded ion control for clocks, so a lattice-clock prize could look like a third helping in the same area. There is also a fair argument that this is a refinement of how well we measure time rather than a discovery of a new phenomenon, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Pierre Lemonde, Martin Boyd and others contributed lattice-clock results that the two credited names do not cover.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because progress is limited by what can be measured and how precisely, and he sees a new way of measuring time confirmed by many laboratories (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN, JILA, NPL), with the redefinition of the second not being required for a prize.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition is not a precondition and that the multi-laboratory agreement is the decisive maturity evidence. Where I add a qualification is his framing of the clock as a new measurement capability: the prize should name the physical idea, Lamb-Dicke confinement with cancelled light shifts, and not the record accuracy number, which will keep moving. I also share his worry about the 2005 and 2012 precedents and think the citation should be written to separate the lattice concept from the comb and the single-ion clock.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened a new observational window, and he treats the diffuse flux, not the individual source identifications, as the Nobel-level result. He ranks lattice clocks second and circuit QED fifth, deferring on circuit QED because of the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I accept his criterion of instrument plus discovery and respect the solidity of the diffuse-flux detection. My hesitation is that his own attribution paragraph concedes the allocation among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA founders is unsettled, and that most of the flux still has no identified origin. That makes it less clean than lattice clocks today, although I defer to him and Danielsson on astroparticle weight and would not oppose it strongly if the allocation is settled. I take his point on circuit QED proximity seriously and it has moved my own first choice.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first, as a genuine clue from nature that opened neutrino astronomy, and puts topological insulators second and circuit QED third. He notes that circuit QED needs to be argued as distinct from the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED has to be argued as a distinct discovery, and I tried to do that in my opening ballot, but I find the committee's repeated caution persuasive. Four colleagues raise the proximity to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis, and a prize for the platform that builds directly on circuit tunnelling within a year of the 2025 prize risks looking like one story split in two. Danielsson is right that the topological-insulator case is conceptually deeper than I weighed it, but his own note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang fall outside the three names is a real attribution problem for me as well.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new classification of electronic states with a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration, and sees the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap as a known allocation problem but not fatal.
responses.response: I agree the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is conceptually strong and has been independently confirmed by ARPES and transport. I disagree that the BHZ problem is minor: BHZ made the specific prediction that told Molenkamp where to look, and Zhang's death in 2018 narrows what the committee can fairly do. I also note that the 2016 prize on topological phases is a closer precedent than he acknowledges, so topological insulators face the same overlap concern that I raise against circuit QED.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first for a minimal, universal mechanism with rigorous theory and decisive experiment, and puts circuit QED second as a timely invention with a coherent theory-plus-experiment trio.
responses.response: His point on circuit QED being a natural theory-plus-experiment trio is fair, and I still think Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf are the right three if the committee awards it. I would qualify his view on timeliness: after the 2025 prize I would prefer a gap, and a decision I take as a Chalmers WACQT director is one where my own proximity should make me cautious about pressing it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Pierre Lemonde, Martin Boyd or other lattice-clock contributors have claims that make a two-name prize unfair.
Whether I am overcorrecting away from circuit QED because of the 2025 prize and my own proximity to that community; a gap of a few years might change my view.
For IceCube and topological insulators, I cannot judge attribution within large collaborations or the BHZ credit as well as colleagues in those fields.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue for B004 (circuit QED). I am a theorist in superconducting circuits at Chalmers, directing WACQT, which has hosted Martinis and Clarke as guest researchers, and I have long professional ties with the circuit-QED community, including Per Delsing's group. I also described Devoret as an influence on my work. For B004 and B012 (squeezing, close to my microwave work) I should be cautious in leading the argument. No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the optical lattice clock community is apparent from my profile.
